Basic Annals (本紀) juan 1–19

1本紀第一世紀 Annals 1 - Prefatory Annals1072–1145

The annals of the nine ancestors of the Jin, from Hanpu to Kangzong. They tell the Mohe and Heishui origins, the migration from Koryŏ, the rise of the Wanyan house as Liao-appointed military commissioners, its wars against rival Jurchen tribes and Koryŏ, and end with the historians' comment. The chapter sets the Jurchen customs, tribal order and Liao relations that precede Taizu's war.

2本紀第二太祖　阿骨打 Annals 2 - Taizu (Emperor Aguda)1109–1123

The annals of Taizu (Aguda, r. 1115-1123), founder of the Jin: his youth and rise among the Wanyan chiefs under the Liao, the break with the Liao and the campaigns that destroyed their empire from Ningjiang to Yanjing, with the first edicts on mouke units, bondage, submitted peoples and the Song alliance, and his death, burial and the historian's verdict.

3本紀第三太宗　吳乞買 Annals 3 - Taizong (Emperor Wuqimai)1121–1135

The annals of Taizong (Wuqimai), the second Jin emperor, 1123 to 1135: his accession after Taizu's death, the end of the Liao, and the invasion of the Northern Song with the fall of Kaifeng in 1126-27. The entries also record relief, settlement of garrison households, the setting up of the puppet state of Qi, embassies and birthday congratulations, and close with the historian's comment.

Annals of Xizong (Hela), r. 1135-1149, from his naming as heir to his murder by Digunai. Records the Qi and Koryo, Xia and Song embassies, the 1141-1142 peace with the Song, reforms of ritual, offices and scripts, disasters and omens, and the purges and drinking of his last years.

5本紀第五海陵　亮 Annals 5 - Hailing (Prince Liang)1144–1180

The annals of the deposed emperor Hailing, Wanyan Liang (r. 1149-1161). They cover his youth and rise under Xizong, the coup of 1149, the purge of the Wanyan princes, the move of the capital to Yan (Zhongdu) in 1153 and the reburial of the ancestors at Dafangshan, the preparation and failure of the invasion of the Song in 1161, his murder by mutinous troops, and his posthumous demotion, closing with the historians' judgment.

6本紀第六世宗　雍　上 Annals 6 - Shizong Part 1 (Emperor Yong)1161–1172

Annals of Shizong, part 1 (juan 6): the emperor's birth and career as Prince of Ge and governor, his proclamation at Liaoyang in 1161 against Hailing, and the first eleven years of Dading (1161 to 1171). It records the suppression of the Khitan revolt of Wovan, the war and peace with the Song in 1165, embassies, hunts and camps, relief and remissions, and the emperor's repeated charges to his ministers on counsel, merit and frugality.

Annals of Shizong (Dading 12 to 20, 1172 to 1180): the Song, Koryo and Xia embassies at festivals, spring-water and Jinlian Chuan tours, tax remissions and relief after floods and drought, prosecutions of corrupt officials, and the emperor's repeated talks on Jurchen old ways, frugality and the choice of officials. 19本紀第十九世紀補 Annals 19 - Supplement to the Prefatory Annals1121–1189

The supplementary annals (世紀補) of the Jinshi for three princes who never reigned, each given imperial rank afterwards: Zongjun (Jingxuan), Zongyao (Ruizong, father of Shizong) and Yungong (Xianzong, Shizong's crown prince and Zhangzong's father). Zongjun and Zongyao are told through the wars on the Liao and the Song, Xianzong through his education, his regency in 1184, his death and mourning, and his character; the historians' comment ends the chapter.

Treatises (志) juan 20–58

20志第一天文 Treatise 1 - Astronomy

The astronomy monograph (天文志) of the Jinshi. After a preface on the value of recording heavenly signs, it lists dated observations by reign: solar eclipses, sun halos and auspicious clouds, then lunar eclipses, planets, comets and meteors. A few entries record court responses, rites at eclipses and astrologers' readings tied to wars and the fall of the Jin.

Topics
Learning, science and technology, Nature
Size
487 verses, 8,708 characters, 2 compiler notes
21志第二曆上 Treatise 2 - Calendar Part 1

The first treatise on the calendar (曆志上). It opens with a short history of the Jin calendars, the Da Ming calendar of Yang Ji adopted in 1135 and the Zhiwei revision of 1171 that served to the end of the dynasty, then gives the constants and rules of the calendar for the sun, moon, solar terms, lodges, gnomon shadows and day length.

Topics
Learning, science and technology, Court and dynasty
Size
328 verses, 10,743 characters, 4 tables
22志第三曆下 Treatise 3 - Calendar Part 2

The second treatise on the calendar (曆志下). It gives the rules of the Da Ming and Zhiwei calendar for the moon's motion, lunar and solar eclipses and the five planets, each under its printed heading, and ends with a history of the armillary sphere and celestial globe from Han to Song and their fate under the Jin.

Topics
Learning, science and technology

23志第四五行 Treatise 4 - Five Phases

The Wuxing treatise (monograph on the five phases) of the Jinshi. After a preface on method, it records omens, strange events, floods, droughts, locusts, earthquakes and fires reign by reign from the Wanyan rise to the fall in 1234, with some memorials and explanations by astronomers.

It opens with a preface on how the Jin acquired, compiled and lost its rituals, then gives the origin of the suburban sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, its altars, and the full ceremony step by step from fasting to the return of the emperor, with two later debates on jade and victims.

136金國語解官稱／人事／物象／物類／姓氏 Appendix - Glossary of Jin Language (Jin guoyu jie) - Official Titles, Human Affairs, Phenomena, Categories of Things, Clan Names

The Jinshi glossary of Jurchen words (Jin guoyu jie), appended to the history. It gives readings and meanings for the Boji lie council offices, meng'an and mouke, officials, kin terms, personal names, common words, terrain, objects, animals and plants, and the Jurchen clan names with their Chinese surname equivalents. Each gloss takes the subject of its term.
